title: How trim_clip.py keeps the last 30 seconds of a video
summary: trim_clip.py makes a short, shareable copy of a video: it keeps only the last N seconds (30 by default) and compresses them into a new MP4. It finds the videos, asks [[ffprobe]] what is inside each one, decides where to cut, and has [[ffmpeg]] write the new clip, which it then reads back to check. The encode has its own sub-workflow, where the picture size and the [[Audio tracks]] are handled.
takeaway: The original is only ever read: `-sseof` makes ffmpeg start near the end, and every result is a new file under a name that is not taken yet.

canvases.title: From your recordings to a short clip
canvases.intro: The whole run, one video at a time. The encode itself is a sub-workflow: open **Make the new clip** to see inside.

explain.what: You start the script from a terminal. It reads the options: which videos, how many seconds to keep, the size limit and the quality.
explain.why: Every later step reads these options, so they are fixed once, at the start.
how: Pass video paths, or `--latest N` to take your N newest recordings.
`--seconds` sets how much of the end to keep (30 by default).
`--max-height` and `--crf` set the size and the quality of the new file.
`--list` only shows what would be trimmed and encodes nothing.
explain.n8n: A Manual Trigger with a small form: the options are the fields you fill in before the run.

explain.what: Builds the list of videos to trim: the paths you gave, plus the newest recordings in your Videos folder when you asked for `--latest`.
explain.why: The script stops before any work if the list is empty or a path is wrong, so a typo never leaves a half-finished run.
how: Walk the Videos folder and keep files with a video extension (.mp4, .mkv, .mov and a few more).
With `--match`, keep only paths that contain that text.
Sort newest first and take the first N.
Stop with a message if nothing is left or a path does not exist.
explain.n8n: A Read Files node, then Filter, Sort and Limit to N items.
gotchas: On Windows the Videos and Desktop folders are read from the registry, so a moved folder is still found. Elsewhere the script uses the folder of that name in your home directory.

explain.what: Takes the videos one at a time. Each one goes through the steps on the right, then the loop moves on to the next.
explain.why: Every video needs its own length check, its own file name and its own encode.
how: Hand the next video to the probe step through the `loop` output.
When the last one is done, leave through the `done` output.
With `--list`, print each video and skip the encode.
explain.n8n: The Loop Over Items node with a batch size of 1.
gotchas: A failed encode stops the whole script, so the videos after it are not trimmed.

explain.what: Every video has been handled. Each new clip sits in the output folder, and every original is unchanged.
explain.why: Nothing is left to do: the lines printed along the way are the report.
how: The script exits normally.

explain.what: Asks [[ffprobe]] three things about the video: how long it is, how tall the picture is, and how many [[Audio tracks]] it has.
explain.why: The next steps depend on these numbers: the length decides the cut, the height decides the scaling, the tracks decide the audio mix.
how: Run ffprobe and ask for the duration, and for each stream its type and height, as JSON.
Ignore a cover picture that is stored as a video stream.
Count the audio streams.
Print a one-line summary of the original.
explain.n8n: An Execute Command node that runs ffprobe, then a Code node that reads its JSON.
gotchas: If ffmpeg is not on your PATH, `find_tool` also looks in the winget install folder on Windows before giving up with an install hint.

explain.what: Compares the video's length with the seconds you asked to keep (30 by default).
explain.why: You cannot keep the last 30 seconds of a 20-second clip. A short clip is kept whole and only compressed.
how: Longer than N: take `yes` and cut to the last N seconds.
N seconds or shorter: take `no`, print a note and keep everything.

nodes.name: Start N seconds before the end
nodes.subtitle: -sseof -30

explain.what: Tells ffmpeg to start reading N seconds before the end of the file, so only the last N seconds reach the encoder.
explain.why: Seeking from the end skips the rest of the recording, so a long video is not decoded from its first frame.
how: Add [[-sseof]] `-30` before `-i`, so it applies to the input file.
ffmpeg jumps near that point and drops the frames before it, so the cut is exact.
The original file is only read, never changed.
explain.n8n: Like a start offset on a read step, counted back from the end.
gotchas: `-sseof` must come before `-i`. After it, ffmpeg treats it as an output option and stops with an error.

explain.what: Leaves out the seek, so ffmpeg reads the clip from its first frame. It is still compressed and resized like any other.
explain.why: Cutting makes no sense on a clip that is already short, and this way every result comes out in the same size and format.
how: Print `shorter than 30s: keeping all of it, compressed`.
Build the command without `-sseof`.

explain.what: Picks a file name that is not taken and runs ffmpeg to write the new MP4. The sub-workflow shows each choice inside.
explain.why: The encode makes its own small decisions (picture size, audio), so they get a canvas of their own.
how: Pick a free name in the output folder (your Desktop by default).
Build the ffmpeg command and run it.
Open the sub-workflow for the detail.
explain.n8n: An Execute Workflow node that calls a sub-workflow and waits for it.

explain.what: Probes the new file and prints its length, height and size, so you can see the cut worked.
explain.why: Reading the result back is a cheap proof: a 30-second cut should report about 30 seconds at 1080p.
how: Run the same probe on the new file.
Print the new path, the length, the height and the size in MB.
explain.n8n: A second Execute Command node that reads the output back, like a check after a write.
gotchas: The length can differ by a frame or so, because video is cut on whole frames.

stickies.text: The original video is only read. Every result is a **new file**, and ffmpeg's `-n` flag refuses to overwrite one.

tour.title: The idea
tour.text: Game recorders save long videos, but the moment worth sharing is usually at the end. This script keeps only the last N seconds and makes them small enough to send.

tour.title: You run it
tour.text: One command with a few options. The defaults keep 30 seconds at up to 1080p.

tour.title: Find the videos
tour.text: Your paths, or your newest recordings. A wrong path stops the run before any work starts.

tour.title: One at a time
tour.text: Like n8n's Loop Over Items: each video goes through the same steps, then the loop takes the next.

tour.title: Look inside first
tour.text: [[ffprobe]] reports the length, the height and the number of audio tracks. Every choice that follows uses these three numbers.

tour.title: Cut or keep?
tour.text: A video longer than N seconds is cut. A shorter one is kept whole.

tour.title: Seek from the end
tour.text: `-sseof -30` starts reading 30 seconds before the end, so the rest of the recording is skipped.

tour.title: Short clips stay whole
tour.text: No seek: the whole clip is compressed, so every result looks the same.

tour.title: Make the clip
tour.text: A free name, then ffmpeg. Open this step to see how the size and the sound are handled.

tour.title: Read it back
tour.text: The new file is probed and printed, then the loop moves to the next video.

tour.title: Finished
tour.text: New clips in the output folder, originals untouched.

runs.name: Two recordings, one of them short

canvases.title: Make the new clip
canvases.intro: Called once per video. It picks the output name, then builds one ffmpeg command piece by piece and runs it.

explain.what: Starts with one video and what the probe found about it, plus your options.
explain.why: Everything the command needs is known before it is built.
how: Receive the source path, the length, the height and the number of audio tracks.
Start the command with quiet logging, so only errors are printed.
explain.n8n: The Execute Workflow Trigger at the top of a sub-workflow.

explain.what: Names the new file after the original plus the length kept. If that name is taken, it adds (2), (3) and so on.
explain.why: Running the script twice on the same video never overwrites the first clip.
how: Start from `<name> - last 30s.mp4` in the output folder.
While that file exists, try `(2)`, then `(3)`.
Hand the free path to ffmpeg.
explain.n8n: A Code node that builds the file name, with a small loop until the name is free.
gotchas: ffmpeg also gets `-n`, which refuses to overwrite, as a second guard.

explain.what: Checks the picture height against `--max-height` (1080 by default).
explain.why: A 1440p or 4K recording makes a big file that many chat apps shrink anyway. 1080p is a good size to share.
how: Taller than the limit: take `yes` and scale down.
At or under the limit, or with `--max-height 0`: take `no` and keep the size.

explain.what: Adds a scale filter that resizes the picture to 1080 pixels tall and keeps its shape.
explain.why: A smaller picture makes a smaller file. The width follows the height, so nothing looks stretched.
how: Add `[0:v:0]scale=-2:1080[v]` to the filter graph.
`-2` means: pick the width that keeps the shape, rounded to an even number.
Encode the scaled picture `[v]` instead of the original stream.
explain.n8n: An Edit Image node set to resize by height.
gotchas: H.264 in the common `yuv420p` colour format needs even sizes, which is why the width is `-2` and not `-1`.

explain.what: Looks at the track count from the probe and picks how the sound is carried over.
explain.why: Some recorders save game sound and your microphone as two separate [[Audio tracks]], and most players only play the first one.
how: One track: carry it across.
Two or more: mix them into one track.
None: the clip has no sound, so no audio is mapped.
explain.n8n: A Switch node with three rules on the track count.

explain.what: Maps the single sound track into the new clip, encoded as AAC.
explain.why: Nothing to mix: one track plays the same everywhere.
how: Map `0:a:0`, the first audio track of the input.
Encode it as AAC at 160 kbit/s.

explain.what: Mixes every audio track into one, each at its own volume, so game sound and voice are both heard in any player.
explain.why: Most players and phones only play the first track. Without the mix, your voice would be silently lost.
how: List every track: `[0:a:0][0:a:1]`.
Add `amix=inputs=2:normalize=0[a]` to the filter graph.
Encode the mixed track `[a]` as AAC.
explain.n8n: A Merge node that combines two inputs into one item.
gotchas: Without `normalize=0`, amix lowers each input so the sum cannot clip, which makes the whole mix quieter.

explain.what: Finishes the command: the video as H.264 at the chosen quality, the sound as AAC, and the file laid out so it starts playing before it has fully loaded.
explain.why: H.264 and AAC in an MP4 play almost everywhere: phones, browsers and chat apps.
how: Join the filters, if any, into one `-filter_complex`.
Video: `libx264`, preset `slow`, [[CRF]] 23, `yuv420p` colour.
Audio, when there is any: AAC at 160 kbit/s.
`+faststart` moves the index to the front of the file; `-n` refuses to overwrite.
explain.n8n: The settings panel of a node: nothing runs yet, the options are only collected.

output.command: ffmpeg -hide_banner -loglevel error -nostats -sseof -30 -i boss-fight.mp4 -filter_complex "[0:v:0]scale=-2:1080[v];[0:a:0][0:a:1]amix=inputs=2:normalize=0[a]" -map [v] -c:v libx264 -preset slow -crf 23 -pix_fmt yuv420p -map [a] -c:a aac -b:a 160k -movflags +faststart -n "boss-fight - last 30s (2).mp4"

explain.what: Runs the finished command and waits for it. [[ffmpeg]] reads the original and writes the new MP4.
explain.why: This is the only step that does real work; every step before it only built the command.
how: Run ffmpeg with the full list of arguments.
Wait until it finishes.
If ffmpeg fails, `check=True` stops the script with an error.
gotchas: Preset `slow` trades encoding time for a smaller file, so it takes noticeably longer than ffmpeg's default `medium`.

tour.title: One video in
tour.text: The video and the three numbers the probe found: length, height and audio tracks.

tour.title: A name that is free
tour.text: `boss-fight - last 30s.mp4`, or `(2)` when that one exists already.

tour.title: Too tall?
tour.text: Anything taller than 1080p is scaled down. Smaller recordings keep their size.

tour.title: Scale, keep the shape
tour.text: The width follows the height and stays even, which H.264 needs.

tour.title: How much sound?
tour.text: A Switch on the track count: one, none, or two and more.

tour.title: One track
tour.text: Carried across as AAC.

tour.title: Several tracks
tour.text: Mixed into one, so a player that only plays the first track still has your voice.

tour.title: The settings
tour.text: H.264 at [[CRF]] 23, AAC sound, and `+faststart` so the clip starts playing at once.

tour.title: Run it
tour.text: ffmpeg writes the new file. Back on the main canvas, the result is checked.

glossary.plain: A free command-line program that reads, cuts, converts and compresses video and audio.
glossary.n8n: The engine behind an Execute Command node in this flow.

glossary.plain: ffmpeg's companion: it only reads a file and reports what is inside, such as the length, the picture size and the streams.
Separate sound streams inside one video file, such as game sound on one track and a microphone on another.
glossary.example: A recording with 2 audio tracks often plays only the game sound in a phone's player.

glossary.plain: An ffmpeg input option: start reading this many seconds before the end of the file.
Constant Rate Factor, the quality dial of the H.264 encoder. Lower is sharper and bigger; 23 is the default.
glossary.example: Around 18 looks close to the original; 28 is visibly softer but much smaller.

outOfScope: How the Windows registry lookup for the Videos and Desktop folders works (`shell_folder`).
